subsubtopic: REQUEST QUOTAS NOT BE IMPOSED ON STEEL WITH LOW CARBON CONTENT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with an important matter of pressing necessity.

March 14, 1979
There is a shortage of building steel with low carbon content in eastern Canada at the present time. The supply difficulties related to a tendency of some companies to set quotas on their existing stocks have led suppliers to increase their prices. Since such behaviour erodes the purchasing power of consumers in the regions involved at a time when they can hardly cope with the new inflationary push, while some companies are making record profits, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That the House forbid those companies to set such quotas on existing stocks so that they may not take advantage of a temporarily reduced production to increase uselessly their prices without reason and boost their profits.

speechtext:

Whereas there are certain parts of our heritage and traditions which are steeped in history; whereas the word "dominion" is such a part of our history, based on the eighth verse of the 72nd Psalm; whereas it is essential to adhere in some respects to tradition and heritage; whereas this fact is recognized in the Holidays Act which declares that July 1 in each and every year is a national holiday and such holiday shall be observed as such; and whereas there has been a tendency for some government departments, and particularly the Department of the Secretary of State and Crown corporations including the CBC, to ignore the Holidays Act, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher):

speechtext:
Yesterday, in the course of discussion of a question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) to which a contribution was made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), a question arose as to a possible discrepancy between various texts of Hansard and the final printed version. As has always been my practice and as I naturally would, 1 undertook to look into this matter on behalf of the House and determine the true sequence of events as they occurred.
Privilege-Mr. McKenzie
The quotation by the hon. member for Athabasca was, in fact, from the press run copy, which is the first rough copy which comes from the reporter's notes. It is not verified by the reporter or by the editor; it is simply a rough copy prepared by the reporter, which has been used by the press but has never been used for purposes of quotation either by them or in the House because of its rough, unedited nature. When the reporter has an opportunity to verify the notes and the editor has examined them, a second copy is prepared. That is the copy generally referred to as "the blues" which goes to the member who is concerned in case any alterations might be required to improve the grammatical sense or the editorial accuracy of those notes before the final version is printed.
In this particular case several changes, as is always the situation, were made between the rough copy which, as I say, is not to be used for quotation, and the preliminary copy, "the blue", the one which is submitted to members for verification. The minister has said in this instance that no alterations were made by her. The alterations which were made were made by the Editor and the Chief of the Branch, Mr. Baker, who as is, thankfully, his usual practice, backs up his own floor reporters by sitting in the gallery and taking his own notes. When he examined the rough copy he made the changes which occurred and he did so because his notes indicated that those changes accurately reflected what the minister had, in fact, said.
Subsequently, since this matter had arisen, I asked him, of course, to verify his version with the sound tape and also with the television tape. He has done so and verifies that his own notes as to what the minister had said were, in fact, accurate. His notes were verified by the sound tape and the television tape. That is why the version in his notes, which appeared in "the blues" and in the final transcript of Hansard, is precisely the language used by the minister on Monday.
I think we have to say in the circumstances of the tumultuous exchanges which can take place in the House of Commons it is a mark of considerable merit to the Hansard reporters, and particularly to the Chief of Hansard that he extends this rather remarkable devotion to the accuracy of the printed word.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion put before the House today by our party reflects what I think is the number one issue among ordinary Canadians from coast to coast. That number one issue is the skyrocketing increases we have seen over the last year or so.
Today we received some further evidence of skyrocketing price increases from Statistics Canada. About an hour and a half ago Statistics Canada announced that the industry selling price for manufacturing in this country went up by 11 per cent from January of 1978 to January of 1979. Just yesterday in the House the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) assured us that a 3 per cent cut in the manufacturers' sales tax had been passed on to consumers and that that is reflected in the consumer price index. When the

minister rises to respond, I hope he will explain how it is that that 3 per cent sales tax cut was passed on when the manufacturing index has gone up by 11 per cent. It is at its highest level since June of 1975. I think the government has been failing on that front as well as many other fronts.
The consumer price index has gone up by some 8.9 per cent. On the other hand, wages increased in 1978 by only 6.4 per cent. In other words, the average standard of living for workers in this country is going down, not up. It is going down largely because a few years ago the Anti-Inflation Board controlled wages but not prices or profits. One need only look at statistics from Statistics Canada on the average weekly wage in 1978 to find that the average weekly wage went up from $252 to $269, which was an increase of less than the increase in the cost of living. If we compute into that the increase in the cost of living, we find that the net loss to the average Canadian worker was some $340 in 1978. So the standard of living in this country has been going down.
This afternoon I want to speak about a number of things which we think should be done. In my opinion the government has not been doing well with regard to a number of things, and I will give the minister some specific examples. The minister is always looking into things. His department does not seem to know its left foot from its right foot. His department seems to exist only for cosmetic and public relations purposes. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is a tame pussycat who just purrs. He has yet to learn how to growl and really mean business when dealing with big companies. There have been increases in food prices, farm input costs, lumber prices, energy prices and automobile prices. I could go on and on.
What has the government's response been to the increase in the cost of living? First of all, we had the Anti-Inflation Board which studies profits and not mark-ups. Then we had CSIP which turned out to be a disastrous little institution. Then we had the announcement the other day that tariffs will be taken off some foods. That made big banner headlines across the country. When we checked with the Department of Finance we found out that the reduction of tariffs, and the removal of tariffs in some cases, will mean a saving of only $10 million to the consumers of this country. That means that if you go out and buy a pound of raisins, it will cost you 1.5 cents less than it did before. It will cost you 2 cents less for a can of tomato juice, and it will cost you 7 cents less for a cauliflower. Some policy!
Then, with great fanfare, the establishment two weeks ago of the National Commission on Inflation was announced. Again I suggest it is nothing more than a public relations effort by this government. It has the power to investigate price increases, it has the power and authority to publicize those increases, but it does not have any power to do anything about those price increases. It is an economic eunuch. At this time we need an economic policeman who could intervene in the market place. It does not have any power to control the price;
March 14, 1979

it does not have any power at all to hold back a price while it is being investigated; it does not have any power to freeze a specific price where there has been some profiteering or some gouging of the public.
As I said, what we need is an agency that is strong. I want to suggest to the minister a number of things which we think must be done if we are to control, to a significant degree, the increase in the cost of living. Our party has spoken about a fair prices commission which would put some teeth into the government's national commission on inflation, which would take the shackles off its feet and which would allow it to have some power and some influence, a commission which would be a small and powerful watchdog with the power to roll back prices when they need to be rolled back. It would have the power to stall a price increase while we are investigating whether or not it is too high. It would have the power to freeze the price for a certain amount of time.
The minister has said to that, "Well, the NDP wants to bring back controls." We are not talking about across the board controls, freezes, or anything of that sort. We are talking about a small body that would have the power, on a selective basis, to stop profiteering or high price increases, and to force rollbacks where rollbacks are deemed to be necessary. I am talking about a powerful little watchdog, an economic hit team which would have the power to go to a bakery, a banking company or an oil company, and say, "Look, we have found your prices to be too high and they should not be that high. You are profiteering, roll back your prices." I suggest they may only look into one out of 500 or 1,000 price increases, but no one will know who will be hit next, and therefore we believe it would have the effect of keeping companies and the market place honest. We do not have that now.
The minister says, "There are all kinds of problems with it. What about the Constitution and prices being under provincial jurisdiction?" I suggest to him that when they brought in the AIB they did not have any problem in controlling wages and getting the provinces to agree. I am sure there is as much an emergency now as there was three years ago when they brought in AIB. We also have other controls in this country. We have a two-price system for wheat, we have a two-price system for copper, and a two-price system for energy. We also have the CTC which controls and regulates prices. What we can do through those agencies and with those commodities, I suggest we can do through the fair prices commission. We can expand our philosophy to the fair prices commission which will have the power, on a selective basis, to roll back prices.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
I would like to give the minister seven or eight specific examples of what we would refer to a fair prices commission, if he had the guts and the courage to set one up in the country. But before I do that I want to mention briefly four other things which we believe should be done if we are going to bring down the cost of living in this country.
Second, we should reinstate the food subsidies which have been taken off by this government, subsidies which were
Price Increases
imposed through the pressure of this party in the minority parliament from 1972 to 1974, food subsidies on fluid milk and on skim milk powder, and put back subsidies on bread and flour which were removed shortly before Christmas of last year. We found that when the subsidy was taken off skim milk powder about a year or so ago, the consumption of skim milk powder in the first six months after the subsidy went off went down by some 56 per cent. Yet the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) says she is concerned about nutrition and the health of young people.
Third, the bank rate in this country has increased by 40 per cent in the last 13 months. We have a bank rate now that is usurious, that is costing the consumers, the housebuilders, and the farmers a lot more money than it should. We are suggesting to the government that there be an immediate reduction of the bank rate by one per cent and a further gradual reduction after that.
Fourth, there is going to be a two step increase in the price of oil by $1 a barrel in the month of July and another $1 a barrel in January of 1980. We said to the government that both these increases should be rescinded. We do not need these increases and therefore we should be freezing temporarily the price of gasoline, the price of home heating fuel, and the price of other petroleum products we get from oil. I am aware that this would create some anxiety among the government's friends such as the Exxon Corporation, but if one looks at their profit figures one finds that we have played Santa Claus far too long in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: Trust Texaco!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: And Mr. Blakeney.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
We are saying that the regulatory agencies in this country should be beefed up and made tougher, agencies such as the Canadian Transport Commission, in terms of the freight rates and in terms of the Bell Telephone rates that are determined by the CTC.
These are five points in summary which we think should be implemented immediately if we are to decrease the cost of living in Canada.
Now I want to give the minister a few specific examples of price increases which we think warrant investigation by an agency which has the power to roll back prices or to control a price temporarily while an investigation is being carried on. These are not very obscure items, as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) says, they are items that have been mentioned to us by hundreds of people across the country, items that people buy when they go into the supermarket to purchase consumer goods.
I want to say that there is a great deal of concern across the way that there will be an increase in the cost of living or an increase in inflation because of big wage demands. I want to say to the government that the most effective way to make sure that workers demand reasonable wage increases is to make sure that the price increases which workers are faced

March 14, 1979
Price Increases
with in supermarkets are reasonable and that those prices are kept low.
First I want to speak about food and the Anti-Inflation Board. In 1978 the price of food went up by 21 per cent. We look at our food dollar. I know that as compared to other countries we do not pay much for our food in terms of the percentage of our dollar. We pay about 16 per cent or 17 per cent and so do people in the United States; in Europe they pay about 20 per cent, in Japan about 30 per cent, and in India about 60 per cent. But when I take a look at the food dollar, I wonder where that food dollar has gone.
Back in 1951, when I was in kindergarten, the farmers got some 60 per cent of the food dollar. But last year, in 1978, the farmers' share of the food dollar has been reduced from 60 per cent to 38 per cent. It is that reduction in the farmers' share of the food dollar that concerns all of us from rural ridings, and it concerns many Canadians because most Canadians do not blame the farmers for the rapid increase in the price of food.
I should like to take a look at some of the specific price increases which I believe the minister should examine. I will start off with turkey. We all remember before Christmas when the increase in the price of turkeys was skyrocketing. We remember the minister saying that farmers were not producing enough; let us open the borders and fly some more turkeys in. That is one turkey who is an expert on turkeys. He said that we need more imports and that there is a shortage of supply. After Christmas and after the supermarkets were restricting the supply to Canadian consumers, we find instead of a shortage that in January there was 22 million pounds of turkey in supply. I believe the minister should have looked into it. He should have had an agency powerful enough to say to the supermarkets, "Look, roll back the price of turkeys. You are gouging Canadian consumers; you are doing it intentionally."
Let us have a look at the price of grade A turkey which is under ten pounds in weight. In the week ending February 9, 1979, as compared to one year earlier, the retail price of grade A turkey went up by some 36 per cent; but the price the farmer receives went up by only 12.5 per cent. The raw product rose 12.5 per cent and the retail price rose 36 per cent. Why does the minister not look into that to ensure that there is an agency to roll back that price to the consumers being gouged?
The same thing applies to the price of chicken. If we compare the same periods of time we will find that the retail price of chicken went up from 69 cents per pound to $1.18 per pound, which is an increase of 71 per cent; while the price the farmer received for producing chicken went up from 46 cents a pound to 53 cents a pound, for an increase of 15 per cent. I am sure it is not the worker processing chicken who received the extra cream. It is not the farmer, but I wonder about the retail companies, processors and people in between. Again the minister rose and talked about a shortage of supply, but the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) set him straight by saying that there were four million pounds more chicken in

storage as of February 1, 1979, than a year ago. Still the price of chicken rose. It is rather suspicious, it seems to me.
I should like to refer to another example, the price of skim milk powder which is needed by younger people, and indeed by all Canadians. The 34-cent per pound subsidy was removed. The farmers received an increase of four cents per pound. The actual price of raw material went up by 38 cents, but when we look at the new price in the supermarkets it was up by 45 cents a pound. Why did it cost an extra seven cents for skim milk products?
Now I should like to deal with beef. We know farmers were being pressured and ripped off with a low price for beef for three or four years in a row, until approximately a year ago. Last year when prices finally started to rise for the farmers, lo and behold, the price started rising faster for the consumer. We can take a look at some of the margins and some of the spreads. The information I am about to refer to comes from the beef information centre. In June, 1978, the average markup on a pound of beef in Toronto was 66 cents, in Calgary it was 72 cents, and in Vancouver it was 94 cents, whereas the mark-up the previous year was 20 cents per pound. I am told by people in the retail business that a mark-up of approximately 25 cents to 30 cents per pound is normal and profitable for supermarkets.
Another example is the price of pork. The minister should direct his attention to this area. In the week ending June 24, 1978, compared to the week ending June 24, 1977, the price of bacon rose 22 per cent, the price of a roast of pork went up 34 per cent, and the price of sausage, which unfortunately a lot of poor people eat because it is one of the cheapest meats, went up by 75 per cent. How much did the price of pork to the farmer rise? The price of pork to the farmer rose 5.8 per cent during the same period of time. We checked out wage increases for packing-house workers and we found the annual wage increase was well within the guidelines established by the Anti-Inflation Board.
Now I should like to deal with the price of bread. Of course we had the intervention of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. In a minority parliament we were able to force the minister to subsidize the price of bread for Canadian consumers. The subsidy was removed because of the so-called restraint program when government picks on the little guy. The subsidy on an average loaf of bread of 3.3 cents was removed, yet in retail stores the price of a loaf of bread rose by seven cents or more. In January the CPI indicated that the average increase in the price of bread was 13 per cent. I say to the minister why? When the price of raw material rises 3.3 cents, why does the price of the final product rise by seven cents? Between December 31 and January 1 wages and other costs did not go up. The price of raw material went up 3.3 cents, but the retail price more than doubled. The minister said he is looking into that matter. I wonder if the minister ever stops looking into anything. I wonder if he ever looks in a mirror to see whether he is being serious as the minister.
Of course the subsidy was removed on flour when it was removed on bread, the subsidy of 22 cents on 5.5 pounds of
March 14, 1979

flour. The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) buys flour for his wife and five children. When he went into the store in January to buy flour he did not find a price increase of 22 cents; if was 44 cents. In the city of Regina the increase in the price of flour was 42 cents. Once again I must ask, why? When the 22-cent subsidy was removed, why was the retail mark-up 44 cents? In other words, why was the retail mark-up twice that of the raw material?
I should like to turn to the other side of farm equation which makes farmers so angry. I have spoken with farmers from all parts of the country, each and every week. When they find out that the price to consumers of the food they produce is escalating while their incomes are dropping or remaining the same, they become angry. For example, the net incomes of farmers in Saskatchewan actually will drop in 1979, while the net incomes of other farmers across the land will not change. This is happening while farm input costs are escalating rapidly.
The minister and his officials should be investigating and rolling back unwarranted price increases. Repeatedly farmers have referred to price increases in parts and repairs on farm machinery. When the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was approached by farmers he was told that a little nut, bolt or part which used to cost approximately a couple of dollars now costs $10 or $12.
I should like to direct the attention of the minister to the specific example of a press drill boot. I tell the hon. Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that a press drill boot is a little metal ending which is on the end of the hose or funnel which goes between the disks when seeds are being planted in a field. The International Harvester press drill boot ten years ago cost $8 each. Approximately three years ago the same little piece of metal cost $27 each. Do hon. members know what that piece of metal costs today? It costs approximately $62. It went up by 129 per cent in three years, and in the last year it went up some 55 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: It must be made of nickel.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: Or gold-plated.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
I know the salaries of steelworkers did not rise that much. Also I know the raw price of steel did not rise that much. I look at the profits of steel companies and I wonder whether the extra dollars being paid by farmers for press drill boots went to the multinational companies in terms of profits. That particular problem was referred by the minister of agriculture in Saskatchewan to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Do hon. members know what the minister said? He said, "I am sorry; we have no power to roll back prices since the AIB. We have set up CSIP to investigate, but there is no apparent violation under the Combines Investigation Act, and we have no power to roll back price increases since the AIB went to the promised land and was buried."
Price Increases
Let me give the minister a few more examples of farm input cost increases that anger my constituents. Let us consider the 100-horsepower tractor, which is a common thing on the farm these days. The average price of such a tractor, according to the department of agriculture in the province of Alberta, went up by some 16 per cent in the last year. That tractor now costs the farmer $28,000. Let us consider the combine which a year ago cost $32,000 and now costs $41,000 for the same model and the same size, but one year newer. That is an increase of some 30 per cent. Is it any wonder that the price of the final product in this country is going up at an alarmingly rapid rate?
Let me give the minister a couple of examples outside the food and agricultural area. The first example I would mention is textiles. I do not know if the minister noticed in the newspaper this morning the report that the price of textiles in this country has gone up by some 66 per cent in one case and 73 per cent in another. I wonder whether he is investigating to see if textile companies have been taking advantage of protective quotas, and whether they have been taking advantage of the reduced value of the Canadian dollar.
Then we have another example in relation to the cost of lumber which has gone up by 80 per cent in the last two years. It now costs about $1,200 more to build a house of 1,800 square feet than it did two years ago, strictly because the input cost of lumber has gone up by 80 per cent.
Let me use the very specific example given by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes). The price of one board foot of two by four a year ago was 17 cents. The price today is six cents more, or 23 cents, an increase of roughly one third. At the same time we see that profits in the pulp and paper industry have increased almost without exception, in many cases to very high levels. At the same time this government has handed over $235 million to the pulp and paper companies.
If we are going to talk about restraint in this country we should make sure it is not practised on the backs of the ordinary citizens, the farmers, the workers, the old and the young. Restraint should be practised on the backs of those who can best carry the burden, the wealthy and the large multinational companies in this country.
I have given the minister a number of specific examples today of things that are of real concern to the average citizen right across this country. I do not want him to get up and say, "I am looking into this", or "I have looked into that". I want him to get up and tell us why he does not go to the cabinet and say, "Look, I need the power to change this National Commission on Inflation from a pussycat to a tiger. What we need in this country is a tough watchdog that can intervene and roll back prices in the market place. We need an agency with that power." I am sure the cabinet would not give the power to him because this minister has no clout.
The main function of this minister is to fulfil a public relations function for the government, making the Canadian

March 14, 1979
Price Increases
people believe that something is being done by the government in terms of controlling prices in this country. The government is not doing that. As much as 1 like the minister personally, and I have known him for years, this is one minister who should be fired by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for incompetency.
In the two minutes I have left I should like to summarize for the minister. I hope he will respond in a serious way and not in the superficial, cosmetic way he has responded in the past. First of all I would like to see the government bring in a fair prices commission to act as a tough watchdog, or a little economic "hit" team with the power to hold back price increases while they are being investigated, to roll back price increases that are unwarranted, and with the power to freeze and control prices on a selective basis for a specific period of time.
Secondly, I want the minister to tell us why the government has ended subsidies on fluid milk, skim milk, bread and flour, those basic nutritious foods needed by each and every one of us, while at the same time it has offered millions of dollars to wealthy hockey team owners for the construction of rinks in many cities of this country, and another $200 million to the pulp and paper industry across the land.
Thirdly, I wonder if this toothless tiger, the minister from Montreal, can tell us why the government does not reduce the bank rate by at least 1 per cent in order to stimulate the economy, reduce the cost of house building and the cost of consumer and farm loans. Can he forcefully tell us whether the government is considering rescinding the $2 increase in the price of oil, that is, the $1 due July 1, 1979, and the second $1 on January 1, 1980?
Finally, will the minister tell us whether the government is going to toughen up the regulatory agencies in this country, like the CTC, in order that they can have some effective control of freight rates, telephone rates and other rates that consumers have to pay? Those are five specific things we believe the government can do. To supplement that, I have given him another ten or 12 specific items that could be referred to-

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to assure you and, through you, the people of this country, that the government is extremely concerned about increasing prices, and places a high priority on finding solutions both in the short and long-term.
I should like to make clear, however, that the problem is one principally caused by rising food prices. If one looks at the recent consumer price index one will see that the large increase

month over month was not caused by non-food items but, rather, by food items. They in turn are principally affected by the beef cycle and the cost of imported food.
What has this government done about that, and what more can be done? I want to make clear that there are no magic solutions to reduce prices dramatically but that with the right programs some price increases can be moderated and others can be stabilized.
Let me give some of the measures that have been introduced by this government to combat inflation. I will list them first and give the details later. From 1975 to 1978 we had the Anti-Inflation Board which did have the power to roll back and control prices, wages and profits. This was followed by the monitoring agency CSIP, the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity, followed by the National Commission on Inflation.
Last year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) announced two sales tax cuts, one in the spring and one in November, which again had a serious influence on curtailing the rate of inflation. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) toward the end of last year announced an increase in the guaranteed income supplement and the family tax credit program to help Canadians of medium and lower incomes.
Another major initiative taken by the government to deal with inflation is our program to curtail our expenses and size dramatically, and I will say a bit more about that later. We also had measures to increase production and supply quotas both in the farm and fisheries areas.
Last week the Minister of Finance announced a reduction in import tariffs on food. I notice in today's Citizen on the front page a headline which states that 39 cent lettuce is on the way. It starts by saying:
After three months of paying budget-breaking lettuce prices, consumers should get a dramatic break this week as most stores lower prices nearly 50 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: Loss leaders.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
This is a general lowering of lettuce prices whereas loss leaders are usually found in one store or another. In addition to these reduced import tariffs, as was mentioned earlier in the day by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) we have had a program to help consumers of oil in the eastern part of Canada with subsidies which have kept prices down for the last few years.
As I pointed out, the AIB was in place for three years. It ended its mandate on December 31, 1978, and it had powers to control prices, wages and profits. While the NDP voted against that measure in 1975, they are now proposing controls with roll-back powers. It is difficult to understand, and they have not explained that position today.
They did the same thing last week when they put forward their other motion with respect to a commission to control and roll back prices. I will ask them now, as I did last week, how
March 14, 1979

can they suggest powers to roll back prices without also granting powers to roll back costs, including wages which are very dear to them? If costs are the cause of the increased price then certainly we cannot control the price without controlling the costs, but the NDP have not explained this or said how they can do one without the other.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: You did it.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: I was listening, and the NDP failed to explain that question on occasion after occasion. Again the New Democratic Party is continually stating and, I would submit, using the big lie technique, that while the AIB controlled wages they did not control prices or profits.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: That is what the conference board said.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: This statement, Mr. Speaker, is absolutely false, and I would like to refer to a few examples. Both wages and prices were controlled by the AIB between the three-year period from October, 1975, to December, 1978. With respect to prices, in 1975 at the beginning of the program the CP Index, excluding food, rose 10.1 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Why
exclude food?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
I will deal with food later. But excluding food, it rose 10.1 per cent. In January, 1979, at the end of the program the comparable figure was 6 per cent. Profit margins of industrial corporations declined from 7.19 per cent at the beginning of the program to 5.2 per cent in the first half of 1978, the last year of the program. By October, 1978, over $264 million in excess corporate revenue had been returned to consumers as a result of action by the AIB. As of August, 1978, the AIB received 377 requests for dividend increases. Of these, 117 cases representing $407 million were refused or amended.
With respect to wages during the period of controls, real disposable income per person employed in Canada grew by 7 per cent in the last three years. In the United States in a comparable period, real disposable income declined 2 per cent. The average weekly wage for Canadian workers rose from $203.32 in 1975 to over $272 in 1978, an increase of 33 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: How much has food gone up since 1975?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
On the whole, Mr. Speaker, the anti-inflation program of the government was successful. It certainly moderated the rate of inflation, and we will never know what the rate would have been without the AIB. We do know that our record over the last five years has been much better than most countries. In any case, the AIB controls are now terminated. All sectors of the Canadian economy agreed that this should be done, including the then NDP government of Saskatchewan and the former NDP government of Manitoba.
Following our discussions with the provinces, we found no support for a post-control monitoring body with investigative
Price Increases
powers, although the Minister of Finance proposed such a body. Consequently, following the consensus of the provincial ministers at the conference, we established the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity at the beginning of 1979. While CSIP did some worth-while work and published some informative reports, it did not have the power to compel information. Consequently, last week the government established the National Commission on Inflation which will have powers under the Inquiries Act and will be able to monitor price movement properly and other phenomena which cause inflation.
The commission will not only have a deterrent effect on unconscionable price increases, but it can highlight them publicly and recommend action to the federal and provincial governments.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
A lot of
good that will do.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Earlier I referred to two tax cuts initiated by the Minister of Finance last year. The first, which related to the provincial sales tax, certainly had a deflationary effect and was considered a success. The second, which is still in force, relates to the federal excise tax and applies to several consumer products. While the inventory subject to this tax cut only came on the market in January, the most recent consumer price index indicates that this tax cut is being passed on. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, the non-food part of the CPI for last month increased moderately, and some products, such as furniture and clothing, actually declined. The federal sales tax cut will continue to have its impact on the economy.
1 also mentioned the increases in the Guaranteed Income Supplement and the new family tax credit. Both will provide additional purchasing power to lower and middle income families and retired Canadians to help them deal with increased prices. This is in addition to the government indexing program for pensions and the guaranteed income supplement.
I also want to repeat again that the government has programs to adjust supply and production in food products when increasing prices are due to short supply. In response to my honourable colleague's remarks with respect to my statements on supply before Christmas and after Christmas, 1 would refer him to bulletins put out by the marketing boards and by the Department of Agriculture which confirm the statements I made in the House at that time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: Were they wrong?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
No, they confirmed that I was correct. The government recently announced new guidelines for the National Farm Products Marketing Council, which is the governing body for our marketing boards. These new guidelines, among other things, directed the council to consider not only the producers' interests but also the consumers' interests. At the same time we appointed a new chairman who was experienced in both farming and the consumer movement and who has the

March 14, 1979
Price Increases
confidence of both groups. Many of our marketing boards had already announced increased production quotas for 1979, but it is yet too early to know their effect and whether they are adequate. In any case, the boards and the council are continually reviewing these matters and can adjust their production quotas when necessary.
I had mentioned the government's program to control inflation by controlling its own size and spending. Hon. members will recall that a year or two ago the opposition was alleging that the cause of inflation was the size of the government's budget and the size of the government's deficit. As the House now knows, for the last few years the government has had a program to keep spending increases below increases in the gross national product and to curtail public employee increases to less than 1 per cent. In the month of August we announced an additional program to curtail our expenses and to keep our government program within reasonable size. Last week the Minister of Finance announced certain cuts in import tariffs on selected foods. A little earlier I referred to an article in today's Citizen which confirms that prices are already being reduced for many of these products. This action is an important measure to help moderate inflation for Canadians.
I get a kick out of the NDP's continual allegation that I am "looking into things". On two or three different occasions during his speech the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) asked me if I would look into this, look into that. Because I am a very co-operative minister I always like to oblige him, and when he asks me to look into something, of course I do so. Today I have outlined a large number of measures which are measures for action.
As I said earlier in my remarks, the causes of the recent and spectacular price increases in food are principally due to the beef cycle and imported foods. As hon. members know, many of our beef producers suffered low prices a couple of years ago with the result that they sold off their herds. We now have very low supplies of beef with a continuing high demand and resultant high prices. It takes about three years to reproduce a herd of beef and we cannot correct that problem immediately. It will take time, and confidence in the beef producing areas of the country.
With respect to imported foods, it is true they cost more because our dollar declined in comparison to the American dollar. During the winter months, if we want fresh fruit and vegetables we must import them from the United States and other countries. Consequently we must pay the extra 17 or 18 cents because of the difference in the dollar. People may ask why we do not do something about this. I suppose we could have pegged our currency and stored it in many ways but that would cost taxpayers a lot of money and would have repercussions in many other areas of the economy.
It is easy to observe that while the lower dollar has had some serious effects on the price of imported food products it has also allowed us to sell a great deal of our production abroad. It
[Mr. Allmand.)
has helped us with foreign trade deficits and is helping to produce the many jobs that were needed in this country.
If the allegation is made-and it has been made-that the recent price increases are due to profiteering or gouging by many of the companies in the food industries, there is just no evidence to support that at this time. There have been inquiries at all levels of the food industry and none have proved that any one level was ripping off, gouging, or profiteering at the expense of another.
The recent AIB report on profit margins in the food industry pointed out that while profits were increasing at the end of 1978, they were not out of line with historical norms. According to this report, over the first nine months of 1978 profit margins in Canada's food processing and food retailing industries varied little from the historical norms. For food processors the profit margin as a percentage of sales has declined significantly since 1973. For the first nine months of 1978 it was 3.3 per cent, equal to the 1974 low. Profit margins of food wholesalers for the first nine months of 1978 average 1.3 per cent compared to 1.21 per cent in the corresponding period of 1977 and the 1971-77 average of 1.67 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: These are facts.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: What about return on investment?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
If we look at the statistics of return on investment we see there has been no spectacular increase, but there have been increases. Generally, the increases in profits in business which have occurred during the last year are a sign that the economy is improving. I think that is a good thing for this country.
A year or so ago members of the opposition were criticizing the government because business was bad. Now that we see reports of increased profits they seem to be criticizing that as well. I say increased profits are a sign that business is on the way up. That will mean more money for government through taxes, and thus more money for social programs and other things.
Of course there will always be bad actors in the business community, and individual companies that will try to rig the market and fix prices. We have had recent examples of this. All hon. members are aware of the action my department took against the sugar companies. We lost that in the trial court but won a record judgment in the Quebec Court of Appeal which condemned those companies for fixing prices, and levied a record fine of $2.5 million.
We recently had a judgment of the court against one of the leading jeans manufacturers when they tried to practise resale price maintenance. They would only distribute jeans to retail concerns and outlets if they sold them at a fixed price, which was against the law. A large judgment was made against that company.
While there has not been profiteering or gouging generally, there have been examples, and there will continue to be examples, of companies that act improperly in the market place.
March 14, 1979

What else has the government done to help consumers with high prices?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: Change the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
That is the only solution the Conservative party has. Last week when the NDP put their motion before the House to deal with inflation and high prices, the spokesmen for the Conservative party had only one suggestion- change the government. They did not say what their solutions would be. As a matter of fact they have criticized the solutions we have put forward.
One thing that can be done to help consumers cope with high prices is to give them good information about food, and especially lower priced foods that are nutritious. Each week we issue information called "Food Backgrounders" which are sent to weekly and daily newspapers. These are used in the "Shop Wisely" and "Best Buy" columns, which are helpful in picking out the best buys from week to week. Where there is price competition in the food retail business it is helpful to have information on where the best buys are available. Despite the high price of beef, for example, pork and poultry have been good buys in eastern Canada in recent weeks. These newspaper columns using our background information encourage Canadians to look at these foods as good alternative sources of protein.
I recently congratulated a group of women in Ontario who set up a program called "Women Against Rising Prices." They are doing what we suggest-being selective in their shopping, refusing to buy products that are too high in price, and they are shopping wisely. We intend to continue with our programs and upgrade them to provide useful information.
Two other programs that can help save money for consumers, which we have supported strongly-as a matter of fact I made a speech to businessmen suggesting these programs before they came into operation-are the "no-name" foods and "no frills" stores. When you compare the price of a shopping basket of "no name" food products purchased in a "no fills" store, you will see considerable savings.
Another program of a similar nature that has been operating for the last two years, and which will operate again this year, is the "Food Talk" program. Last year we sent 40 or 50 teams into lower income areas, immigration areas, native peoples areas, and different areas which require information, to show them how to make the best buys in the supermarket. This helped them considerably to improve their food purchasing and to deal with their food budgets.
When the NDP presented their motion on this subject last week I stated in my speech that one of the measures I hoped to bring forward soon is the competition reform bill. When 1 said that, 1 did not intend it to be a solution to the short-term problem of rising prices in February and March, 1979. It should be obvious to the many commentators and critics that reform in competition laws could only help in the long run. None the less, it is an important reform. As I said last week, if you really want fair prices in the marketplace, your best guarantee is an open and competitive marketplace. I cannot
Price Increases
understand how many people misunderstood my putting that forward as a short-term solution. That was never my intention.
I should also like to remind the House that even under the present law the competition bureau in my department has been taking many actions and has been successful in many prosecutions. I mentioned a moment ago our actions with regard to the sugar industry and the jeans and clothing industry. For example, since the beginning of 1978 the department has had 19 prosecutions covering conspiracy, merger and monopoly, and 112 convictions in the areas of deceptive trade practices and resale price maintenance. We have also had prosecutions in many other areas of fraud and price fixing, the weights and measures program, the electricity and gas program, and so on.
I still intend to come forward with the competition reform bill. I hope it will soon be ready for the House. However, it will be a measure to deal with fair prices in the long run and not in the short run.
My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), recently released some interesting information with regard to food and food prices. In a very useful little booklet that was published, he pointed out that from 1971 to 1977 the average hourly earnings in manufacturing in Canada increased 94.5 per cent. Over the same period the price of food increased 80.1 per cent. On average, one hour of work in manufacturing would buy approximately 8 per cent more food in 1977 than in 1971.
Other interesting information that the Minister of Agriculture has provided is that in 1949 it was necessary to work 20 hours to feed a family of four for one week. In 1959, one had to work 14 hours to feed a family that size. In 1977 one only had to work eight hours to buy the same amount of food. Even though food prices were higher in 1977, it took less than half as long in 1979 to buy food for a family of four for one week.
The Minister of Agriculture is extremely proud of this government's record in helping farmers become more productive, and increasing supply in this country. I support him 100 per cent on that. Critics in the opposition pretend there is some difference of opinion between the Minister of Agriculture,'the Minister of Fisheries, and myself. They are completely wrong. We believe that in the long run the best guarantee of a good source of food is a sound and satisfied production community, whether it be in farming or in fisheries.
I wish to point out a few other matters that should be brought to the attention of Canadians when talking about high food prices. When we go into a supermarket and look at the full and long shelves of products, we note that many of the shelves are not filled with food at all but with cigarettes, tobacco products, and pet food.
1 understand that the pet food business in this country, as well as the cigarette and alcohol industries, is a billion dollar industry. These industries are certainly not declining. It is hard to understand criticism from the opposition about how poor Canadians are when we continue to increase our spending for

March 14, 1979
Price Increases
pet food, alcohol, restaurants, cosmetics, entertainment and so on.
Again referring to some of the remarks of my good colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, I note that he is very quick to point out the great waste of food in this country, the amount of food thrown out each day from our restaurants, homes, and banquets. When we look at these kinds of things we find some of the criticism by the opposition a bit hypocritical.
The NDP motion before us today is just another political gimmick. As I said before, when they had a chance to vote for price controls and roll-back powers, they criticized them severely and voted against them. This is not a serious measure they have put before us, but merely a hypocritical con game. As for the Conservatives, their only solution to the cost of food and consumer goods is to have an election. They have no policy at all.
In conclusion, I assure the House and the country that the government will take every reasonable step to combat inflation. However, we have no intention of bringing back controls or introducing measures which might bring short-term relief but result in more serious damage to the economy in other areas, especially with regard to employment and production. Now that those things are improving considerably, we want to see that improvement continue.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion of the New Democratic Party quite properly addresses attention to an increasing concern on the part of Canadians about increases in the cost of living. As the hon. member who moved the motion properly noted, one of those components is the increase in the cost of food.
It was fascinating to listen to the minister criticize the Conservatives who want an election, and to describe his own program. He started off by saying he was concerned. That is a detailed program of the government-they are concerned when something is wrong. He said that another part of their program was that they wanted more information. They have had ten years of more and more information. There has been no action, but all kinds of information. The government has just appointed a new agency which will provide more information.
The minister said that another part of his program was to encourage consumers to shop wisely. I point out to him that shopping wisely is not a solution to increases in the cost of living. It is a defence by people whose budgets are being wasted away by soaring prices. It is not a government program. It is a necessary defence by consumers across Canada.
The minister said part of his program was to welcome and encourage no name and no frills stores. Finally he mentioned "Food Talk". That is a program that completely describes not only the program but the record of this government for the past ten years. All they have done is talk about it. We have food talk from the minister, "Mr. Alltalk."
The minister mentioned 112 prosecutions. He talked about prosecutions in the area of weights and measures. A few weeks ago I raised the question of prosecutions over delivery meters

on home oil heating trucks. The minister still has not explained why out of all those 500 meters that were rejected so totally by his department that the people owning those trucks were put out of business until the meters were corrected, that out of that total they found during an eight-month investigation, they prosecuted exactly five people. The fines for those who were prosecuted were enormous. The biggest one was $600. The minister has been avoiding the issue. Now he seems to be avoiding the debate by leaving the chamber. It is at least consistent. A driver or operator of a home heating oil truck being fined $600 is like getting a licence. He could steal $600 by noon without half trying.
The specific proposal that the New Democratic Party has made in this motion, as is not untypical of the NDP, deals only with the symptoms. It proposes a band aid to deal with an amputation. While the consumers of Canada are bleeding to death the NDP has a band-aid to propose. Nevertheless, they do identify a real concern on the part of Canadians-soaring prices. The talk we have heard from the minister this afternoon is typical of a long line of talk and empty promises, and non-performance which has persisted ever since this government took office. Canadians were promised a food strategy in the speech from the Throne of the 1974. That promise has not been kept.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was going to "wrestle inflation to the ground". That was in 1974. That promise has not been kept. That was four years after he had told us inflation no longer exists. First, it no longer existed, then he was going to wrestle it to the ground and presumably, now, Canadians are expected to live with it.

speechtext:
It is clear that monitoring inflation has done nothing to moderate it. Indeed, the cost of administering these bodies may actually have added to the problem. For example, the AIB which was supposed to have 200 employees ended up with a staff of more than 600. The government spent more
March 14, 1979

than $70 million dollars on running that agency in the three years of its lifespan.
There were a couple of important paragraphs in the Speech from the Throne of February 1974:
The government is developing a policy on food based on the following objectives: an adequate and dependable supply of quality food for a growing population in Canada enjoying a rising standard of living: reasonable food prices for the consumer, in not requiring an undue proportion of income for Canadians to secure a sufficient and balanced diet, and for the producer in providing a return adequate to encourage production of food items which can be produced economically and efficiently in Canada.
Since that promise was made, food prices have risen by nearly 60 per cent and they are expected to rise a further 20 per cent this year-that is the figure the minister himself has used. Instead of devising a food strategy, the government has held a food conference to give the appearance of doing something. Over the last six years since 1973, while inflation rates have continued between a minimum of IV2 per cent and a maximum of almost 11 per cent, in only one of those years was the rate of increase in the food prices below the general increase. In all the other five years increases in food prices led increases in the cost of living. Food prices in Canada have more than doubled since 1971. They will have tripled by 1981.
If these general figures are horrifying, selected figures published by Statistics Canada about individual items are even worse. In the last two years beef has gone up by 82 per cent, that is, between January of 1977 and January of this year. Ground beef has gone up by 116 per cent; powdered skim milk by 76 per cent; grapefruit by 58 per cent; oranges by 96 per cent; canned orange juice by 55 per cent; celery by 57 per cent; lettuce by 161 per cent; tomatoes by 55 per cent. The list is endless. The price increases are horrifying. And what do we get from the government? More rhetoric, more agencies to study the problem, more information.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the information does not have to come from government agencies; Canadians do not need another agency to enable them to find out what is happening to food prices. Those prices are published in the newspaper every single week. Every supermarket in the country takes advertisements like the one I hold in my hand to tell people what is happening to prices. And here is the bad news: instant coffee $4.88 a jar, iceberg lettuce, on special, 49 cents a head. Every newspaper tells the same story. That one is from Ottawa; this one is from Montreal. Spaghetti and macaroni, two 500 grams boxes $1.00; bananas, 4 pounds for a dollar; bread, 3 loaves for $1.29; sirloin tip roast, $2.88 a pound. Those prices are from the Montreal paper.
Here is another page. In this case the supermarket has the gall to head the advertisement "low prices". These are loss leaders, by the way, but even so the prices are horrifying; tomatoes, two pounds for $1, lettuce, 2 heads for a $1. Over here we read: bacon, $1.69, round steak, $2.58 a pound, tomato juice, 59 cents for a 48 oz. fluid tin. But the worst thing about this advertisement is that it shows right there just what those prices were last week before certain goods became "specials" and what they will be next week after these special offers are over. That tin of tomato juice was, and will be, 76
Price Increases
cents instead of 59 cents; the steak was $3.08 not $2.58, the bacon was, and will be, $2.08, not $1.69; the lettuce was, and will be, 99 cents a head, not 50 cents a piece. Tomatoes were, and will be, $1.49 for two pounds instead of $1.
And here is the solution, Mr. Speaker; the minister has been quoted as saying Canadians may have to buy more nutritious and less expensive alternatives. He talked about some of the items other than food which are available on the shelves of the supermarkets. Well, here are some of them, here is what Canadians who find that the price of people-food is too high can buy: cat food is only $1 for five tins, dog food is two tins for 89 cents. Now if you stop drinking milk, for instance, if you stop wasting money on that and drink water and eat dog food, you can cut yow food bill way down.
The minister talks about carping criticisms from this side of the House. He cited an article in the newspaper-it was the only one he mentioned-praising what he had done. I should like to read a selection of clippings from newspapers across the country published not only in the last couple of weeks but over the last couple of years and dealing with this department and this problem. The Ottawa Citizen, for example, calls the NCI a "cynical election ploy". The Toronto Sun calls it a "pre-election gimmick". It says the whole concept reeks with cynicism. Again, from the Toronto Sun:
The finance minister said as long as some companies would not co-operate we had to assure the public we could find out what was going on. In other words, the minister does not know what is going on.
The Ottawa Journal called it "a mitigated disaster", whatever that means. There was John Gray writing in the Ottawa Journal-"Let Commission No. 5 Wrestle Inflation to the Ground". He went on: "The Liberals have latched on to the obvious; it is easier to monitor inflation that try to control it". Don McGillivray, writing in the Montreal Gazette, said the new selection body is just an election ploy. In his opinion the NCI has as much hope of stopping inflation "as a walnut has of stopping a steam roller." George Bain in a column headed "The Eleven Years War on Prices" had this to say:
There are married couples buying groceries today who had not reached puberty when this government first started talking about new competition legislation six consumer and corporate affairs ministers ago.
The following appears in The Globe and Mail:
Warren Allmand's rhetorical rage at rising prices is as pretty a piece of political hypocrisy as has come out of the Liberal government so far this election campaign.
The Montreal Star said, and I quote:
There is only one thing certain about Warren Ailmand's proposed threepronged attack on rising prices-it won't do anything to stop prices from rising.
The Winnipeg Free Press said:
-the inflation which has been primarily the cause of depleted financial reserves originated almost exclusively with government.
Talking about the serpent of inflation, the Hamilton Spectator said:
-the commission was empowered to say "tsk, tsk" unto the people and shame the serpent.

The Globe and Mail said:
Canada's consumer price index advanced by 9 per cent last year-a bigger increase than in most other industrialized countries.
It is not just the current press which is critical. Here is something from the middle of last year in the Financial Post:
The most striking feature of the Economic Council of Canada's inflation-analysis group is the care that has gone into ensuring its role and impact will be limited.
On March 1, 1974, the Montreal Star printed the following:
Prime Minister Trudeau said yesterday the government is considering measures to help protect savings from erosion by inflation.
The criticism does not come just from the press and this side of the House. Some of it comes from the other side of the House. A member sitting on the Liberal side told anyone outside the House who would listen that he felt the government was jeopardizing its election prospects by failing to act decisively to provide clear protection against rising prices. The member to whom I refer is the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), a former member of the cabinet. Although he objects to rising prices, what he really objects to with regard to government inaction is not that it does not do anything to help the consumer but that it is jeopardizing the government's re-election chances. Here are some headlines about the minister himself. In 1979: "Allmand Talks Tough on Inflation". "Talks" is the operative word. In 1978 in the Star Phoenix: "Whelan, Allmand Disagree Over Higher Meat Imports".
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is quoted as saying:
And don't blame us if the price tag is further inflated because of currency conditions.
That is the same minister who removed the subsidy on powdered milk and drove the price up 50 per cent and sales down by 50 per cent.
Here is another headline from last year: "Allmand Orders Investigation". "Allmand May Probe High Business Profits". "Allmand's Strategy on Rising Prices Includes a Stronger Inflation Agency". "Allmand Aims to Curb Food Prices". "Consumer in the Boardroom". "Allmand Promises Close Watch". "Improve Machine Food". "Consumer Minister Has Been Consumed". The minister deserves an award for understatements for saying, "I'm not an expert in agricultural economics."
We have had many agencies and much talk. We have had eight ministers of consumer and corporate affairs since this government took power almost 11 years ago. Four of those ministers were in office one year or less, seven of them for under two years. By all counts the present minister is the least competent. He is the one who most often claims that he is misquoted, misunderstood or misinterpreted. He did it again this afternoon in his speech. While he refuses to accept responsibility, he points at processors and distributors. Are they to blame? Perhaps just a few of them. The minister points at producers. Are they to blame? Well, maybe some, but certainly not the bulk of them. He points at consumers. Are they to blame for rising prices? Have they been shopping unwisely? Have they been eating too much? When the minister points a

finger at someone else, he should realize that three fingers are pointing at himself.
This government has done nothing for the past ten years to deal with rising costs of living and, in particular, food prices. The government has made noise. A hen makes a noise when she lays an egg. This government has laid and egg, but it is cackling as if it laid an astroid. We have had Five agencies, eight ministers, hundreds of promises and thousand of occasions on which to act, but we have had zero performance. We have had dithering indecisiveness. This government and this minister have been as organized in their approach to the problem as a kitten with diarrhoea. Just as prices are soaring again, this government, which has consistently postponed an election which would be a real test of its record and its so-called policies, gives us more rhetoric, more promises, and another agency. The only area in which it is not consistent is that the Prime Minister has not appointed another new Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It is about time. This one has been minister for a year and a half.
The government also has the gall to tell the Canadian people there is a light at the end of the tunnel. We have news for the government. The light it sees is a train. A national food policy is overdue. If this government refuses to grasp the nettle and to work on a co-ordinated national food policy which would mean fair prices for consumers, an equitable and efficient distribution system and adequate returns for producers, then let it resign and go to the people, and they will elect a government which can do that. There are five government departments and agencies which presumably have some responsibility in this area, the Canadian Wheat Board, The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Fisheries and the Environment, the Department of National Health and Welfare and others. One or two of the ministers responsible drifted in and out of the House earlier in the debate, but none of them are here at the present time. If they had any real concern or any real policies, surely they would be here to respond in person to this motion presented by the New Democratic Party.
In 1972 there was an all-party committee of this House which reported a year later recommending a ten-year national food strategy. The Food Prices Review Board recommended a food strategy. The Consumers Association of Canada has recommended a food strategy, and this party, as well as our companions to my left, have recommended a food strategy. We are past the point where the problem needs looking into. We are past the point of talk. I challenge the government to do one of two things, either produce concrete proposals which it has the guts to put into effect now, or resign and let the people of Canada elect a government which will do those things.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate on the motion put forth by my colleague the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). It is quite obvious that for the last ten years inflation has become a real psychosis and remains a major
March 14, 1979

hurdle in our attempts to reach our collective and individual goals. In 1975, while we were debating Bill C-73 on anti-inflation, I stated that the austerity measures contemplated by the government did not really go to the heart of the problem. I also added that the efforts that were to be made over the next three years would not solve the problem. The government is now clutching at straws as far as inflation, unemployment and the economy in general are concerned. It is almost recognizing its inability to overcome fantastic price increases such as we have witnessed.
When the prices and wages control program was proposed, the aim of the Anti-Inflation Board was to bring inflation down to 6 per cent over a two-year period. Yet, our rate of inflation remains between 8 and 9 per cent.
This situation is as unacceptable as our unemployment rate and the present economic situation. Mr. Speaker, recently an Ottawa newspaper reported these words of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). In 1970, the Prime Minister said that inflation was no longer a problem in Canada. Some time later, in 1974, he stated: We are going to wrestle inflation to the ground.
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately it is inflation which has wrestled our bank accounts to the ground and robbed the savings of Canadian taxpayers. Since the Liberal government came to power in 1968, inflation has taken fantastic proportions. To contain inflation, the government has offered us a multitude of great promises and a series of five boards which were all supposed to defeat inflation once and for all.
Mr. Speaker, it should be noted that the measures taken up to now, that is, government expenditure restrictions, wages controls and the review of consumer price increases, are only measures. It is about time that someone in the government show some leadership and not be afraid to take the action required.
Food price increases affect a large proportion of family budgets. For many Canadian families, housing and food account for up to 70 per cent of total expenses. The Canadian Senate established the poverty line according to this criterion. Only the families whose income is lower than the average family wages are considered poor. In 1977, 882,000 single people and 1,288,000 families of two or more people were placed in this category. This is an unfortunate situation, Mr. Speaker.
A multitude of organizations have been established to remedy to this situation, including control boards, study commissions, review boards, the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity, and the latest, the National Commission on Inflation announced on March 2 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). What can we expect from this new commission? Certainly not fairer prices! Will it do more than all the others before it? I would like to say yes, but I would be deceiving myself. This commission will only be another smokescreen to hide the ineptitude and indecision of the government.
Price Increases
It will be responsible for supervising changes in prices like all its predecessors, but with a little something added. I refer to the press release of March 2 published by the minister for the duties of this commission. In addition to supervising price changes, the inflation commission will inform the public about the inflationary process.
I guess Canadians need to learn or to learn over again that inflation has been gnawing at them for nearly 10, 15 years. I think every good Canadian is aware of that cancer that keeps gnawing at him. On the other hand, it is really interesting to know that Canadians are not informed about inflation. If they do not know yet what the inflation which is eroding every pay cheque is all about, the commission is going to show them. We are really lucky. We are faced with excessive inflation particularly in food prices but now we will know why our cheque is not big enough to meet the daily needs of our families and households. Then the mandate of the commission will be to identify price increases. It will be a very understandable task for a commission on inflation to carry out, and if it considers it appropriate, it will report to the government and its report will undoubtedly go and join all the others somewhere on a shelf until the government decides to disband it and create another one. Mr. Speaker, I took a couple of pokes at the new commission because it seems to me the establishment of these countless commissions on inflation has become a real joke. It creates false expectations every time, and in spite of that, inflation continues unabated.
If it turns out the government cannot come up with a real energy policy to bring inflation down, must one conclude that it gave in to the financial power of banks and big business? It is often said in government quarters that our inflation comes from abroad, that it is an international phenomenon. That may be true but only in part and it is not a valid reason not to do anything. I would like to remind you that industrialized countries like Switzerland and Germany are doing very well at this time. The ever increasing costs of energy and food we have been experiencing will only be aggravated by the fall of the dollar because those products are imported in large quantities. I think the fall of the dollar is due to a lack of confidence in financial and international banking quarters in our economic situation and the total lack of leadership to straighten it out.
The inflation that continues and will continue to affect us is due for a large part to the past mistakes of monetary and fiscal authorities. Unfortunately, the longer the inflation problem lasts, the more complex the contributing factors become. That is why we should not wait any longer to act. We cannot eternally rely on just our simple measures to counter the reduction in purchasing power. To get to the causes of the disease we will need a round table of management, labour and government representatives to draft a plan of action. I believe that procedure would not benefit one group to the detriment of others.
