speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the member for parliament for Wellington I am responsible for a constituency that is primarily made up of the city of Guelph, which makes up 85 per cent of that constituency and yet is surrounded by a very rural, agricultural area. There are four townships in the riding which make up the balance, the other 15 per cent of the riding. One hundred per cent of my riding, whether it be the city urban or the rural people, are consumers, but the 15 per cent in the rural townships, which are situated on primarily class one and class two agricultural land, are also largely producers. So I have in my riding both consumers and producers whom I represent, and 1 try to represent both groups responsibly. I am not a consumer or producer advocate. I like to think of myself as a constituent advocate.
I was born in the United Kingdom and lived there during World War II. As many hon. members will realize and appreciate, during World War II energy, food and many other materials in the United Kingdom were in very short supply. Thus we had to learn to live, or some may say, exist on the essentials of life. Therefore, one can imagine how amazed I was when I came to Canada in 1947 and saw the phenomenal amount of waste in energy and food. It was absolutely extraordinary the temperature at which buildings were kept, with windows open letting all the heat escape. Also, the amount of food left on plates at the end of a meal and the amount thrown into the garbage before reaching the table were extraordinary. It was prime food, food the people in the United Kingdom could not afford during the war.
At very long last we are coming to our senses, certainly in the area of energy. We realize we cannot continue to be wasteful, that energy is much more important in our economy. This was brought primarily to our attention by the OPEC actions of 1973. The message of conservation finally sunk in, and we are seeing tremendous decreases in the rate of energy consumption. The increases of the past have been lowered by a substantial amount, a little over half the rate of increase in the past. The same should happen in the area of food.
The cost of food in Canada is among the cheapest in the world. Even though it is cheaper, there is no excuse to waste it. We should conserve it. It will be a big job educating the public on the value of nutrition. I am pleased the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and her department have issued booklets which do an excellent job in the area of nutrition. Also I am glad the University of Guelph in my riding has a department which is very concerned with nutrition. That department is helping to educate the public on the importance of nutrition and good value for their food dollar.
Recently I made a suggestion to the Minister of National Health and Welfare to help in the education process of the general public. My suggestion was to adopt a system somewhat similar to the one brought into being by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in the area of labelling

clothes for washing and drying. All items of wearing apparel have recomendations as to how they can be washed and dried; what temperatures should be used; what detergents and bleaches can be used; and what articles can or cannot withstand.
Keeping in mind the expense involved, perhaps it would be a good idea to implement a similar type of labelling as far as food is concerned. Thus, when a person goes through a supermarket, he or she would see what produce was high in vitamins, protein, carbohydrates and other important ingredients for a nutritionally balanced diet.
Also the situation would be helped if consumers paid more attention to buying Canadian. As well as maintaining nutrition, we could assist in the area of imported inflation where we are bringing goods into the country over which we have no control of the prices and therefore the inflationary tendency they promote. For example, as far as vitamin C is concerned, we do not have to drink orange juice every morning. We grow an awful lot of apples in Canada and make an awful lot of apple juice. There is just as much vitamin C in Canadian apple juice as in orange imported from Florida. Many people enjoy apple juice as much as orange juice. How many people think, every time they drink a glass of orange juice, that they are not buying Canadian and that they could help their costs and the economy by switching to apple juice? How many people drink tea and coffee in Canada, but we produce an awful lot of milk. Today we must advertise milk so that it can compete with all other available drinks in the market place, whether they be soft drinks or alcoholic beverages.
I am glad to see the Department of Agriculture is looking into other areas of imported products which can be displaced by growing them in Canada and therefore cutting down on imported inflation. I was pleased to hear about the experiment of growing peanuts in the agricultural land of southwestern Ontario which previously was used to grow tobacco. That experiment is now reaching the commercial stage. We import $50 million worth of peanuts every year. With the devaluation of the dollar which has taken place in the last few months, the price of our imported peanut butter or our imported peanuts which go into peanut butter has increased by that amount of money. If peanuts are grown in southwestern Ontario, which now is economically viable, Canada would not have that inflationary tendency because of the imported product.
There are other areas in which we are still behaving like fat cats. I am very ashamed that we have to bring into the country 8,000 agricultural workers a year to harvest our crops. We cannot find Canadians who are willing to pick crops at harvest time. The farmers must get their crops off the fields within a very short period of time if they are to reap the nutritional benefits of freshly-ripened crops. We cannot find Canadians to do this job, so we must bring in people from the Caribbean or Mexico do do it. With record high unemployment we bring in approximately 8,000 people from outside the country.
When I was going through my teenage years, I made money every summer. My sole source of income as a student was from going into fields and harvesting agricultural crops. There was no shame in that. It was a good experience. That is the free
March 14, 1979

enterprise system of work. By taking positive action to replace imports over which we have no control of price increases, we can tackle inflation caused externally. Recently the National Commission on Inflation was brought into being to pinpoint these problems and to separate external inflation from internal causes of inflation. But the consumer is still the key player in this game; he or she has a choice to exercise. He or she does not have to buy a product in the supermarket. Consumer boycott is one of the most effective weapons of the free enterprise system.
There are other choices. We can grow our own food. We can use it while it is fresh during the harvesting season, and we can freeze the balance to use during the rest of the year.
Approximately 40 per cent of the population of Wellington riding is of ethnic origin. A number of my constituents have very large gardens. Quite frequently they grow tomatoes and peppers of varieties foreign to Canada. They use these unique vegetables in the preparation of their national dishes. I am amazed at the size and the frequency of these gardens. I am amazed at the amount of crops grown to supplement their year-round food consumption and not just during the peak season.
Consumers have another choice. If they do not want to grow their own food, they can go out and pick it. Many farmers have systems whereby people can pick their own food. They can use the food when it is fresh during harvest season, or it can be frozen and used during the balance of the year. For example, my family goes out and picks strawberries in June, corn in August, and apples in September or October. We have the produce fresh when it is in season, and freeze it for use during the rest of the year. Techniques are readily available. If a person does not have such information available, he or she can obtain it from the Department of Agriculture. That department produces booklets containing helpful advice on freezing produce.
There are various manners in which consumers can help in fighting the battle of inflation. The last thing we need is another layer of government bureaucracy. I would not want to see another group looking into the details in order to find out what should or should not be done. There are too many people interfering in the free enterprise system. We should keep government involvement to an absolute minimum. It would keep the cost of government down and it would give the free enterprise system a chance to work. The free enterprise system will work if we use all the tools available, and that includes consumer choice.
I should like to make a few comments concerning some of the facts dealing with immediate food price increases. Food price increases are expected for the first part of 1979, with price increases declining later in the year to keep 1979 price increases to the 12 per cent-14 per cent range, compared to 12.8 per cent for 1978, 8.4 per cent for 1977, and 2.7 per cent for 1976. The 1979 AIB retail survey for February shows higher retail prices for beef, bread, bakery products, fresh fruit and vegetables. Price increases in these areas can be expected for a few more weeks.
Price Increases
What are the causes for these price increases? Canadians are dependent upon foreign supplies for 35 per cent of all fruit and vegetables they purchase. In the wintertime they are dependent for about 75 per cent of their produce on foreign sources. About one third of all price increases is created by agricultural conditions that are unavoidable, whether they be weather conditions, crop failures or cyclical shortages. About one third of all price increases reflect devaluation of the dollar, reductions in subsidies, or marketing arrangements to ensure supply. These are policies necessary for economic growth, increasing employment, and ensuring the consumer food at reasonable prices.
The cost of food to Canadians is a story of which we can be very proud, indeed. In 1978 a U.S. study showed that 13.8 per cent of disposable income was spent for food in Canada. In most countries people spent at least 20 per cent of their budget on food, with people in some countries spending up to 50 per cent. Are we spending more and more every year in real terms on food? No, Mr. Speaker, we are spending less and less every year in real terms of work for the family food basket. The number of hours work required to buy food for a family of four for one week has gone from 20 hours in 1949 to 14 hours in 1959, to 11 hours in 1969, and to eight hours in 1977.
The percentage of disposable income spent on food at home has gone from 20 per cent in 1949 down to 18 per cent in 1959, to 14.6 per cent in 1969, and in the first three quarters of 1978 it was 12.9 per cent.

Yes, the whole lot, just about.
Have food prices increased too quickly? Let us examine some statistics for the 1968-78 period, the last ten years. Gross national product per capita in current dollars has increased from $3,506 in 1968 to $9,873 in 1978, an increase of 182 per cent. Personal disposable income per capita in current dollars has risen from $2,262 in 1968 to $6,629 in 1978, an increase of 193 per cent. Labour income per person employed has gone from $5,063 in 1968 to $13,236 in 1978, an increase of 161 per cent. However, food, according to the consumer price index, has gone from $92.8 in 1968 to $208 in 1978, an increase of 124 per cent, compared to the 161 per cent, 193 per cent and 182 per cent for the other indicators I have given. Food increases, by any measure, have lagged substantially behind income increases.
What about the recent increases in food prices? Available statistics show that in the first three quarters of 1978 food prices increased 11.3 per cent for food at home, while per capita disposable income increased 23 per cent in the same period. During 1976 and 1977 food price increases were almost the lowest of all price increases in consumer purchases. In the same period the cost of energy increased almost four times.
How does Canada compare internationally? Numerous international food surveys have found Canadian food prices among the world's lowest. For example, a January 3, 1979,

March 14, 1979
Price Increases
United States department of agriculture survey found that Ottawa stores charged 21 per cent less than Washington stores for a representative 21-item food basket. In the same survey Canada is shown to have the lowest food prices in terms of average hourly industrial wages of any of the 16 national capitals surveyed. The survey reveals that in Ottawa we pay S3.36 per kilogram of boneless chuck roast while in Washington the cost is $4.01, in Paris it is $5.03, and in London it is $4.38. We have similar statistics here in respect of a dozen eggs, a kilogram of butter, a kilogram of bread, and a kilogram of potatoes.
How long do we have to work here as compared to those in these other places in order to purchase the same amount of these articles? Again, for a kilogram of boneless chuck roast in Ottawa we must work 37 minutes whereas in Washington the figure is 33 minutes, in Paris it is one hour and 32 minutes, and in London it is one hour and 39 minutes. The figures for a kilogram of potatoes in the same comparison are: five minutes in Ottawa, six minutes in Washington, six minutes in Paris, and seven minutes in London. For a dozen eggs the work time figures are: eight minutes in Ottawa, seven minutes in Washington, 27 minutes in Paris, and 24 minutes in London. The figures in respect of a kilogram of butter are: 26 minutes in Ottawa, 34 minutes in Washington, one hour and 23 minutes in Paris, and 46 minutes in London. By any international standards one wants to use, and this is from the United States department of agriculture, foreign agriculture figures, we have a very good record.
How are we dealing with food price increases? Although food price increases are largely unavoidable, the Liberal government recognized the disproportionate burden placed on the poor and the aged and has acted to help these groups through the Child Tax Credit Program and increases in the Guaranteed Income Supplement. The Liberal government has also been indexing pensions and other benefits since 1974.
To monitor further the making of excessive profits at the expense of the consumer, the government has recently established the National Commission on Inflation.
Mr. Speaker, that is our record, and I think we can be proud of it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this motion today although I am not impressed by its content or intent. It is good in theory but simply impossible to implement. It does, however, provide us with an opportunity to discuss the issue and to place the blame for these dramatic price increases where it rightfully belongs. If hon. members on the other side of the House do not agree with me, I am certain the Canadian people will when I indicate that the blame belongs squarely on the shoulders of the present government.
Prices have increased dramatically in respect of most, if not all, goods and services. The reason for these price increases is not unknown. There is nothing mysterious about this, it is obvious. They can be related almost entirely to failures on the part of this government.

What are some of these failures that have resulted in these price increases throughout the whole Canadian system? Let me list some of them as follows: this government's continuing failure to manage the Canadian economy with any degree of success or competence; this government's failure to control inflation; this government's failure to do anything about record high interst rates; this government's failure to produce the kinds of programs and policies that will encourage a greater degree of self-sufficiency in domestically produced agricultural commodities; and this government's failure to produce the kinds of programs and policies that would reduce the reliance of the Canadian consumer on foreign food supplies. Those are some of the major ones. This government's failure to develop a national food strategy or a national food policy has to be one of its major failures.
When we consider the record of this government and its lack of appropriate programs and policies, is it any wonder that prices have escalated in the manner in which they have over the past few years? This government is completely incompetent in all areas within its jurisdiction and its responsibility. Its record clearly indicates that short-term, stop-gap measures, tinkering and political posturing will not relieve the problem in respect of rising prices or in respect of increasing food prices.
The latest example occurred on Monday with a tabling of the ways and means motion relating to the tariff changes. This government had the recommendations of the Canadian Horticultural Council, the producers of fruit and vegetables in this country, and the report of the tariff board for five years, since 1974. Now, five years later, and in the dying days of this parliament and of this government, we finally have those tariff changes trotted out by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) with great pride and great fanfare, trotted out to be the answer to food price increases and to bring great savings to Canadian consumers.
I say that it is complete nonsense. These savings when applied translate into savings which amount to from one cent to seven cents on each item purchased. There are many examples, some of which were cited earlier today. Let us look at cauliflower which is currently selling at $1.50 a head. It would now sell for about four cents of five cents less. The prime example is orange juice. A 28-ounce can will be reduced from 70 cents to 69 cents, a total saving of one cent. We must remember though that that same can of orange juice increased in price by 250 per cent in a relatively short period under the programs of this government.
These tariff changes are nothing but political posturing and mislead the Canadian consumer into believing that it is a solution to the food price problems. Canadian consumers will soon realize that it is simply another futile attempt on the part of this government to avoid the real culprit which, of course, is the government itself and its actions. These tariff changes provide no significant benefit to those in domestic sectors of the food chain. They provide no assurance to producers that Canadian farmers will be able to remain in business, let alone
March 14, 1979

grow and expand their production. In fact many of them are left without protection.
These tariff changes provide no real encouragement to the Canadian food processing sector so that they can grow and expand their operations. In fact the Canadian processing industry will be lucky if it can maintain its present status. If government programs do not ensure the growth and development of Canadians and Canadian businesses, whatever they might be, the results are bound to be disastrous.
We have approximately one million people unemployed in Canada today. The cost to Canadians of this unemployed sector is tremendous, particularly in terms of lost potential and lost opportunity. With the right kind of leadership we could employ well over 100,000 more Canadians in our Canadian food system alone. Let me illustrate my comments by referring to a recent study done by the Canadian Fruit and Vegetable Processors Association. In that study they selected 21 fruit and vegetable items, all of which could be grown in Canada. The total imported value amounted to $92.5 million. The total man hours lost by the Canadian production and processing industries was over 13 million man hours, and the total wages lost was recorded at $51.5 million. It was estimated that the cost to Canadians and to the imbalance of trade would be approximately $110 million. It should be noted that these figures were based on the Canadian dollar when it was at or close to par with the U.S. dollar. These figures are far more significant in terms of 85 cent dollars.
Had these 21 fruit and vegetable products been grown, processed and moved through our Canadian food chain, the additional per capita cost to the Canadian consumer would be a grand total of 48 cents a year. Considering the volume of food imports and the 85 cent dollar, this 48 cents annual per capita cost to consumers would be reduced to an even more insignificant figure today.
When one considers these factors, the loss in jobs, wages and productivity, and the cost in terms of unemployment insurance, the 85 cent dollar, the degree of our dependency on imported foods and the cost to the Canadian consumer, one realizes that the total approach to this problem has been fragmented and not in the best interests of the Canadian farmer, food processor or consumer. Clearly, policies of this government have led to an underutilization of Canadian resources, Canadian facilities, and Canadian labour.
Agricultural exports increased by a mere 7 per cent in 1977 figures over 1976 figures. Agricultural imports, however, increased almost twice as much, up by 13.7 per cent from 1976. Our agricultural trade surplus decreased by 15 per cent. Surely the message is clear. If we continue this trend, we continue to travel the road to disaster. We are in need of a comprehensive and well co-ordinated national food policy. There are dozens of policies at all levels of government which affect food production, processing, distribution and consumption. In fact if one wants a good example of non co-operative federalism or non co-ordinated policies, it would be hard to beat the array of legislation and regulations affecting the food system in this country.
Price Increases
I do not believe that it would be an exaggeration to say that there are more than 20 separate federal departments, not to mention the various divisions within those departments, with regulatory authority over some aspect or another of the food system. With this kind of confusion of responsibility, jealous empire guarding remains a major deterrent to the development of a national food policy. It is with regard to this background that I have a fundamental concern, and it is questionable that we can afford to leave the food sector any longer without an over-all direction or framework within which activities and planning of all governments and the private sector can be based. We, as Canadians, have been blessed with a variety and an abundance of highly nutritional food, but our potential remains almost unlimited. However, drastic cost increases place in question the continuation of this long enjoyed or taken for granted fact.
Taken collectively, the various elements of the Canadian food industry constitute a very large portion of our total national economy and, in addition, a significant contribution to our balance of trade. Unfortunately, as a result of the policies of this government in recent years, Canada has a lesser share of the domestic market and a greater dependency on outside sources for food supplies. We see the serious pressures and lost potential that affect most, if not all, members of the food chain, and that would include consumers as well.
Over-all, when we disregard dollar values, agricultural output has seriously declined in absolute terms over recent years. The gap between achievement and potential for agricultural and food production is widening. Statistics reveal that we had the same level of productivity in the period 1972 to 1974 that existed ten years earlier. This slow growth in food production relative to demand has also shown up in a decline of food exports, to which I referred earlier, in volume terms, and an increase in volume of imports.
The old theory, still very much in practice by the government, of consumer savings by price regulations controlled by food imports, just does not bear up under close scrutiny and examination. Mr. Speaker, if it does not bear up now, where would we be if totally dependent on imports and totally at the mercy of outside suppliers of food?
To be successful, Canada's agriculture and food policy must be enconomically based. It should stimulate development and growth in production, processing and marketing. Emphasis on the latter should apply both at home and abroad. Senior levels of government must agree that the object should be to maximize the development of agriculture and food industries, thus strengthening the whole Canadian economy. It must ensure that not only fair and equitable returns are secured for the primary producers but also to all sectors of the total food chain. It must ensure as well a safe and adequate supply of nutritional food for Canadian consumers at acceptable prices. Mr. Speaker, this goal cannot be achieved by the kinds and types of programs pursued by this government.

March 14, 1979
Price Increases
The confusion and conflicts within this government have served no useful purpose whatsoever. This government has pitted producers against consumers and vice versa. It has polarized these two sectors of our society. It has prompted and promoted distrust among Canadians. Producers need consumers; it is they who purchase the produce. Consumers need producers; it is they who provide the required food and food products. We must narrow the gap and promote a better understanding between producers and consumers. We must work in concert, not in conflict with these two sectors of our society. I am confident that producers, processors and consumers will accept their responsibilities and rise to the challenges that face them.
What is needed is a government with the will, a government with the desire and ability to manage our economy, to control inflation, to lower the rate of unemployment, to encourage a greater degree of self-sufficiency in the agricultural and food industries, and to reduce dependency on foreign food supplies.
Canadians know that the major culprit in the whole food price issue is the government. "You can fool some of the people some of the time, but you cannot fool all of the people all of the time." Canadians are not going to be fooled any longer. This government will get that message, hopefully in the not too distant future when someone over there shows some leadership and musters enough courage to pull the plug and go to the country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity of participating in the debate today, on the motion presented by the hon. member of the New Democratic Party for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) who, on behalf of his party, criticizes the policies of the government which he finds inadequate to control inflation, specially where foods are concerned.
That subject is of particular interest to me, Mr. Speaker, as I know it quite well, having had the privilege of sitting, in 1974 and 1975, on the parliamentary commission whose mandate it was to look into the cause of the inflation which was affecting our economy, and namely food prices. In 1975, after anti-inflation measures were adopted, I participated, in the House of Commons, in the debates on decontrol measures, an exercise considered as extremely complex, which was applied from April 1975 till very recently, the end of December I believe, when the Anti-Inflation Board was dissolved.
Mr. Speaker, for quite some time our policy has been aimed at slowing down and even at controlling inflation while avoiding other types of adjustments in our economy. Those are always difficult steps to take to maintain a very precarious balance. I will not suggest today that we have completely succeeded in reaching our aim which is to reduce the rate of inflation, but I think that if we objectively consider the situation, there is evidence that we will obtain better results at the price level, and that anyhow they are better in Canada than in most other industrialized countries.
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that there were a few failures in the process. They are essentially beyond our control. But even in that case we are trying to respond and to get over them. We still have much to do as is the case in other countries, but I would like to insist on the necessity of keeping confidence in our economy, because if we consider the conditions, such confidence is warranted. Moreover, I notice a more optimistic attitude toward our economy even if it does not show among members opposite or among some economists.
Let us examine briefly what happened inflationwise. About five years ago, Canada, like other countries, was hit by galloping inflation which forced prices up by almost 11 per cent in 1974 and 1975. This situation forced the government to launch its anti-inflation program in the fall and to establish regulations which contributed to the slowing down of rising prices and gradually bring the situation back to normal. But we all recognize that such a control program is mostly a psychological weapon that works well within a free market economy only if it is enforced for a limited period. For this reason we started the decontrol process about a year ago, last April.
That same month the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) said in his spring budget speech that in his opinion the consumer price index would rise some 7 per cent in 1978. In fact, the rise was 9 per cent, and the difference is mainly due to higher than predicted rise in the food prices and to a new decline of the dollar which has raised the price of all imported goods. Save for an unexpected surprise, we believe the CPI will go up by 7 or 7.5 per cent this year, and again, for the most part, this rise will be attributable to food prices and imported goods. I am not for a minute suggesting such a rise is acceptable, but it will be lower than the inflation rate we have known these past years.
Following the lifting of controls, it was decided in a conference of the first ministers to ask the Economic Council of Canada to continue analysing the situation in terms of prices and costs. This request has led us to the establishment of the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity. This agency was given the task of watching for prices and costs changes so as to inform Canadians of any tendency which could possibly thwart our chances to fight inflation. Its terms of reference also included studying structural problems, likely to cause rising costs and prices, thus making the economy more vulnerable to inflationary pressures. Very recently, Mr. Speaker, the CSIP management wrote to major corporations to ask them for information relating to their costs and prices, in order to be able to make more extensive analyses.
This is covered by its terms of reference. I must emphasize however that the first proposal submitted by the federal government to the various premiers at the federal-provincial conference of February 1978 was to grant larger powers to that body in order, not to roll prices back, but to investigate, obtain

March 14, 1979

information, and so on. Quite frankly, it was the provincial premiers who rejected the idea, they asked that we do not proceed with this. New Brunswick's premier suggested he would favour a less powerful agency. Because of changes that were made, there should be more reference to control boards because that term had a coercive connotation. He wished an organization would be established that would operate on a voluntary basis.
There is dissension, Mr. Speaker. Provincial governments do not want us to establish an organization that would be more powerful than the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity. I would point out that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and cabinet are seriously scrutinizing the centre's role, as to whether in particular it should be given certain powers of control to determine in the eyes of Canadians whether some firms are making excessive profits. Whatever the decision, there certainly will be no roll-back powers. We have no intention to go along that road, because we have reasons to believe this would be wrong. In the final analysis, the only way to wrestle inflation is to have a strong and dynamic economy, and to implement a sound fiscal and monetary policy. This is the only way to ensure total recovery and growth in the private sector.
In agreement with the provinces, the government undertook some years ago to control its expenditures, to maintain them below the growth rate of the gross national product. This is what we have been doing. Monetary policy reflects our concern with inflation. A great number of other strong influences are acting to stimulate business in the private sector. We are in a position, Mr. Speaker, to demonstrate that our competitivity has improved at the international level. Our production costs have decreased at a time when the value of our dollar declined on foreign markets. There has been a spectacular increase in the number of jobs-more than 440,000 jobs created during the last 12 months-and in 1978 we recorded an unprecedented surplus of $3.5 billion in our trade balance. The manufacturing sector strongly recovered last year with a production growth of 9 per cent and a job creation growth of 7 per cent.
We are confident that this year the real growth will reach the 3.5 per cent mark and the known intentions of prospective investors allow us to believe that the rate of real investments will go up by 4.5 per cent for the economy as a whole. Frankly speaking, I see nothing wrong with profits, a word which someone dared pronounce. I think it is a very important aspect of the economic crisis our country has gone through namely the fact that profits are increasing. It is the main source of capital and investment required to create jobs, preserve them and generate the growth so badly needed in our country. All sectors in our economy, workers and businesses alike, should feel happy that there have been profits because without them there would not be enough money available for the workers to earn decent wages and keep their jobs.
Price Increases
Mr. Speaker, we believe that everything needed is there to ensure a steady expansion in our economy. We are indeed worried about the price escalation of imported food products which contribute to the lowering of available income of workers. We do not deny either the fact that because of the increase it will be more difficult to reduce inflation. Yet we must ask ourselves seriously if we can actually protect the Canadian people from all the elements of inflation which find their origin abroad. Any overzealous attempt to intervene in the operation of the market when there is nothing to substantiate allegations of price rigging, as here in the case of food products, would indeed be a step in the wrong direction. We would stand the risk of losing the advantage which we painfully acquired in recent years.
The federal government has been subsidizing oil supply in eastern Canada for the last three years in order to maintain an equitable price across the country for this product which represents over $1 million per subsidized day for consumers in eastern Canada. Mr. Speaker, I sympathize with the reasons which motivated the hon. member of the NDP to propose this motion to the House today. I myself, as well as the consumers whose interests I defend, have had enough of unending price increases. All of us on the government side want to do something to help consumers, both collectively and individually, and in the last few years we have indeed done much to ease the burden of soaring prices.
Only recently, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has increased the guaranteed income supplement and instituted a $200 child tax credit aimed at helping poor and middle income Canadians. We reduced the sales tax and personal income tax, directly or through indexation. The latest consumer price index figures demonstrate that the federal sales tax reduction announced in the November budget is in fact felt at the consumer level, and that because of this measure, non-food products in the index have shown only a slight increase. In some cases, there has even been a reduction in the price index of clothing and furniture.
The first and most important measure taken this year to stop inflation was the establishment of the Anti-Inflation Board in the fall of 1975.
The government recently appointed a new president to the National Food Products Marketing Board. He has experience not only in agriculture but also in consumer products. It gives a chance to all food producers to be better heard. The board has received new directions and has been asked to listen attentively to the representations and to consider each case with flexibility.
The government has taken measures to show the food product consumer how to get more for his money. We have sent to daily and weekly papers, news releases showing the better food buys. Last week, for instance, we had a long article about the price of pork which was advantageous in many areas of the country. At other times, we recommend the substitution

of other protein foods like eggs, poultry, and fish. This information is helpful to consumers.
Inflation is certainly a serious matter of concern for the government, but it should not be to the extent that the flexibility and adaptability of the Canadian economy might be comprised. The government is confident that businesses and unions also want to protect the gains made during the three year fight against inflation.
The government has full control over its spending; wages demands and agreements are more realistic, and our export prospects are excellent. Quite possibly food price increases will come down with time. In those circumstances we would be wrong to revert to confrontation, as the motion before the House today suggests, rather than insisting on moderation and seriousness. Canadians know they could not improve their capacity to meet competition and their standard of living just by increasing prices. The government will certainly not tolerate an irresponsible attitude about price and salary increases nor will it resort to control on monetary policy to discourage those inflationary surges. Mr. Speaker, in spite of the inflation we have all been experiencing, it is unfair to say that the average family is helpless against those temporary increases. If we look at the statistics of the past three years, we see that in 1975 an average family of four needed 24 hours of work to buy its grocery basket, 14 hours in 1976 and 8 hours in 1977. So you see that family income went up during those years and the government as a result of the indexing of social benefit payments like old age security pensions, family allowances, welfare, veterans pensions and others has maintained the purchasing power, as the Prime Minister suggested recently, of those who can least cope with inflation. In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I will say that among industrialized nations Canada is still the country which is best coping with the economic difficulties facing industrialized nations today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my remarks this afternoon I want to take members through an average day in the life of a constituent of mine and compare that average day in 1973-74 in terms of what that person is going to be spending in 1979.
Let us start with him waking up in the morning and finding himself in his house. His house in 1973 in the city of Toronto cost $40,605. That was the average selling price of a home. In 1979 that same person wakes up and, if he wants to buy a house and is not fortunate enough to live in one, he finds that the price of the average house in Toronto is $68,500. That is. an increase of $28,000 in the average selling price of a home in the past five and a half years.
He is heating himself either by fuel oil or natural gas. Look at the price of fuel oil. In 1973 it was 25.9 cents a gallon. In 1978-79 it is 60 cents a gallon, an increase of more than 100 per cent. The price of natural gas would have been $1.23 per

thousand cubic feet. Now we are looking at $3.09, an increase of nearly three hundred per cent.
He gets out of bed and makes himself some breakfast. If he has not got cholesterol like the government he might cook himself some eggs. In early 1973 he would have spent 71 cents for a dozen eggs. In February of 1979 he would be spending a $1.05 for the same dozen eggs.

speechtext: They would be a little old by then.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: That is true. They would not taste as good, but they would be more expensive. speechtext: A little stale!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
A little staler and more expensive. If he gets into his car, if he can afford to buy a car, in 1973-74 it would have cost him between $3,000 and $4,000, that same car would be selling now for $5,000 or $6,000. He would be paying, in 1973, 56 cents per gallon. In 1978 he would be spending 93 cents a gallon, and we predict that next year he will be paying over $1.00 a gallon for that gasoline.
If he was taking public transport in the city of Toronto in 1974 he would have spent 30 cents cash fare, or four tickets for a dollar. In 1979, thanks to the policies of the federal and provincial governments and the subsidies for urban transport which were supposed to come according to a promise in 1974 and never came, that same person would be spending 60 cents cash fare. That is double the price, or six tickets for three dollars.
Now what has happened to wages as he gets to his place of work? When he arrives at his place of work does he find that his wages have in any way kept up with the rise in the cost of living? No, Mr. Speaker, they have not. That person would have gone into controls in 1975, he would have been zapped by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), but he did not see his food prices being zapped. And when he finally comes out of controls three years later not only has he not managed to keep up with inflation but he has fallen behind.
We also note that as we come out of controls we have not seen a wage explosion in Canada. There has not been the kind of explosion that the Prime Minister has said he was worrying about. But there has been a price explosion and a profit explosion as we come out of controls, and there is no protection for the Canadian consumer when that happens. None whatsoever.
That individual may then decide to have some lunch, let us say a tin of salmon. Let us go back to the shopping List. In 1973 a tin of salmon would have cost him 72 cents, now it costs him $1.59. If he has a hot dog it was 92 cents a pound in 1973, and $1.72 in 1979. If he decides to be healthy and have some vegetables, tomatoes cost him 49 cents in 1973, and 89 cents in 1979. It is very easy for the Minister of Justice (Mr. March 14, 1979

Lalonde) to laugh. But let me say this to members on the government side. Take a walk down the streets, visit the supermarkets and talk to the people who are in those stores. Talk to the pensioners who have to buy single fish fingers because they cannot afford to buy the entire package, finding it is too expensive and uneconomical to do it that way. We are not simply talking about the cheaper cuts of beef.
There are times in my riding when I know that people are buying food which is not intended for human consumption. Yet the government has removed the subsidies from bread, skim milk, flour and milk which would provide the kind of protection and the kind of subsidy which would guarantee lower prices to those Canadians. Ask those people how they feel. They are terrified. They know they have no control over what is happening to food prices. They know they have no control over what is happening to house programs. They do not have a government in Ontario which is prepared to listen to them or do anything about the cost of public transport. There is a price explosion in the city of Toronto right now and this government has no policies to deal with it.
If you are not feeling too well and decide to go to a doctor in Toronto, look at what OHIP fees would have been in 1973- the chances are your doctor would have been in OHIP in 1973. If you are single person you would have been paying SI 1.00 a month; it was $22.00 for a family. In 1979 the OHIP charge for the single person has risen to $19.00, and for a family it has gone up to $38.00. In May of 1978 a charitable organization known as the Ontario Medical Association set its own fee schedule for doctors, 30 per cent higher than the OHIP fee schedule. In January of 1979 that same charitable organization increased its schedule by 6.94 per cent. In the city of Toronto a quarter of the doctors are no longer in OHIP and are charging the OMA schedule. So health costs are skyrocketing.
If people are not elderly and are forced into a hospital and have to stay longer than 60 days, in the city of Toronto they will be spending $9 a day for the pleasure of living in one of those luxury hotels which we call hospitals. That is the attitude of this government and of the provincial government of Ontario. That is exactly what is happening, and if there is a common agreement between these two parties it is that in an atmosphere of cutting back government expenditures it is respectable to allow doctors to go back into the private sector. This government has made that kind of attitude respectable because of the cutbacks which have taken place.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot quite let that pass. I think a mistake was made. The federal government has not allowed anything like that to happen. Doctors are opting out voluntarily because fees have not been raised for ten years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member can raise points of procedure, but if he disagrees with the hon. member who is speaking, he can seek the floor in due time and make his own remarks.
Price Increases

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the point is that when we look at what has been controlled over the past five years and what this government has done to the ability of people to protect themselves on the private market, it has taken protection away.
The government has controlled wages.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: Come on!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: The Conference Board in Canada said this, not the New Democratic Party. The Conference Board in Canada has pointed out that the government managed to control wages in the period between 1975 and 1978, but not prices. Now that we are coming out of controls we can see that the Canadian public is being subjected to a price and profit explosion. That is why the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) moved this motion today. The people of Canada are beginning to recognize that it is not good to move from one impotent commission to another. It is no good to set up a series of institutions, none of which is effective in dealing with the problem of controlling prices. It is far more important to introduce a government institution which has policing powers and roll-back powers to enable the people of Canada to have the sense of protection and security they need.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: Dreamer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
If the Government of Canada is saying that it is dreaming on the part of the Canadian people to expect to have reasonable prices and not to have gouging and profiteering, I say that the hon. member is in for a nasty surprise. The people of Canada are not dreaming when they expect that kind of treatment. They expect decent treatment. If the hon. member is saying that it is dreaming to expect security, I say he is sadly mistaken because it is not dreaming to expect security. That is something the people of Canada expect and dearly want to have. They are looking for a government and a group of people who are prepared to provide that.
The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville pointed out that instead of having a toothless watchdog which does not even bark any more, we should have a commission which has these policing and investigative powers and also the power to roll back. The people of Canada are looking for an Elliott Ness to protect them at this time, but they have been given an Inspector Clousseau in the person of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand). The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is not even responsible for the National Commission on Inflation. The minister is not even a member of the Board of Economic Development Ministers. His only role is to come into this House on the eve of an election and announce that he will present a competition policy.
The Liberal party has had 16 years to present a competition policy. Every time the government prints up and sends to the business community a competition policy and it gets on the order paper, it is withdrawn. Each time the minister says that the government cannot make up its mind and that each policy is not good enough. He says we need another one which is different. Mr. Basford, who has left this House, proposed a

March 14, 1979
Price Increases
competition policy which was supposed to make the Canadian economy competitive, give some protection to the Canadian consumer, and provide some work. He had to withdraw that policy because of the attacks of the business community.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext: The NDP fought that too.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Then the government set up the Bryce commission on corporate concentration. That commission said that corporate concentration is good for the Canadian people and that we should have more of it. That is the direction in which this government is moving. One day it says one thing, and the next day something different. The government cannot make up its mind about any policy, and the minister has the nerve and the gall to come into this House and say that we need a long-term strategy to deal with prices and that that involves a competition policy. We do not have a bill. The government does not have any ideas. For all we know, such a policy has not even been approved by the cabinet. Once it is approved by the cabinet it probably will not be approved by the business community, to which this government is so beholden.
A shopping basket of 15 items cost $10 in 1973. In 1979 that same shopping basket costs $20.87. That is an increase of over 100 per cent. Unfortunately for this government, the Canadian people buy food every day and every week, and every time they buy food, this government is indicted because it has not had a food policy, a food strategy, a price policy or a price strategy for the past 16 years. This government has gone from pillar to post, and the only controls it ever introduced were controls which got at the so-called villain, wages. Wages were controlled, but nothing really happened to inflation. We had three years of wage controls which did nothing to protect the average consumer, and they certainly did nothing to protect the average wage earner. I say that the people of Canada expect a fair prices commission which would provide them with security, protection, and guarantees against gouging, profiteering and price increases. Hopefully there will be an election soon which will allow the Canadian people to have that institution.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-CONDEMNATION OF INACTION WITH RESPECT TO PRICE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a couple of minutes, but I was very disappointed in the last speech. I was amazed at some of the figures the hon. member used. He picked a price for one food item but missed other food items. Everyone knows, for instance, that if a hot dog cost 78 cents in 1973, one could probably buy one for $1.78 in one store but perhaps $1.40 in another, as I did a week ago. Some of these things do not really count. I think I should point out that increases in prices and increases in wages even themselves out.
I will defend the wage and profit control program which we had because it did control both. It did involve price rollbacks. That is an important point which we must remember. I would like to know how, in this day and age, and with millions of

commodities on food shelves and other shelves, one could actually control prices. There is only one way I see that that could be done in any intelligent way, and that is by controlling wages and profits because they are manageable. Those things are manageable, but prices are not so manageable because of bureaucracy, our relationship with the provinces, constitutional considerations, and so forth.
I have just a few seconds left, and I cannot say very much, but I think the motion before us is very impractical.
The present monitoring body at least has the power to subpoena, to obtain information and so forth, and with proper advertising and proper information to the public the squeeze can be put on those who are profiteering.
